name: Domain-transform methods
text:
# Domain-transform methods

Also called: Fourier-space techniques, frequency-domain methods

## Overview
Domain-transform methods solve the problem of high computational complexity in spatial-domain volume rendering by transforming volumetric data into an alternative domain (typically frequency, [compression](#4-compression.md), or wavelet) where projections can be generated more efficiently [S1, unofficial][S2]. Unlike object-order methods that rasterize primitives, these techniques compute a global transformation of the entire volume, extract a slice or representation in the transformed domain, and inverse-transform to obtain the final image [S1, unofficial][S2]. This approach reduces per-view rendering complexity from $O(N^3)$ to $O(N^2)$ (disregarding the one-time preprocessing cost), making it suitable for interactive X-ray simulation and medical imaging where occlusion effects are not required [S1, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md, unofficial]. The primary drawback is the inability to interactively modify display parameters such as opacity or lighting after the initial transformation [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All domain-transform methods follow a three-stage pipeline: Global Transformation, Slice Extraction (or Domain Evaluation), and Inverse Transformation [S1, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md, 895-hartley-transform-for-memory-reduction.md, 5396-dct-based-volume-rendering.md, unofficial].

1.  **Global Transformation:** The input 3D scalar volume $f(x, y, z)$ is transformed into a global representation in an alternative domain. For [frequency-domain methods](#9801-frequency-domain-methods.md), this is a 3D [Discrete Fourier Transform](#2288-fourier-transform.md) (DFT) or [Discrete Hartley Transform](#6335-discrete-hartley-transform.md) ([DHT](#10048-detached-hybrid-transparency.md)) [S1, 6324-hartley-transform.md, unofficial]. For compression-based methods, it involves transforming coefficients into a compressed block format [S2, 5396-dct-based-volume-rendering.md]. This step is performed once per volume and has a computational complexity of $O(N^3 \log N)$ using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithms [S1, 841-gpu-based-2d-fft.md, unofficial].
2.  **Slice Extraction:** A 2D [slice or projection](#1507-2d-visualization-from-3d-grid-slow.md) is extracted from the global representation corresponding to the desired viewing direction. In frequency-domain methods, this relies on the **Projection-Slice Theorem**, which states that the 2D Fourier transform of a projection is equal to a central slice of the 3D Fourier transform perpendicular to the viewing direction [S3, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md]. Since the slicing plane rarely aligns with the discrete lattice of the transformed [data, interpolation](#7180-data-interpolation.md) (e.g., trilinear, tri-cubic, or windowed sinc) is required to resample the data onto a 2D grid [S3, 952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md].
3.  **Inverse Transformation:** The extracted 2D slice is inverse-transformed back to the spatial domain to produce the final 2D projection image [S1, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md, unofficial]. For frequency methods, this is a 2D Inverse FFT (IFFT) or Inverse [Hartley Transform](#6324-hartley-transform.md) [S1, 6324-hartley-transform.md, unofficial].

**Common Pitfalls:**
*   **Boundary Artifacts:** Transforms assume periodic boundary conditions. Discontinuities at volume boundaries cause high-frequency artifacts (ghosting). Mitigation includes [zero-padding](#6382-zero-padding-for-aliasing-reduction.md) the volume by a factor of $k_2$ (typically $4/3$) and applying vignetting correction (premultiplying by the reciprocal of the interpolation filter response) [S4, S5, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md].
*   **Aliasing:** Insufficient output resolution violates the Nyquist criterion, causing aliasing. The output resolution must satisfy the bandwidth of the volume [S2, 952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md].
*   **Fixed Parameters:** Once transformed, parameters like opacity and lighting cannot be changed interactively, as the transformation is linear and global [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering](824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md)
An [indirect volume rendering](#3314-indirect-volume-rendering.md) technique that generates attenuation-only, X-ray-like projections by exploiting the Fourier projection-slice theorem. It solves the problem of high computational complexity in spatial domain ray-casting by transforming the volume into the frequency domain once, then generating views via 2D resampling and inverse transforms, reducing per-view complexity from $O(N^3)$ to $O(N^2 \log N)$. Unlike [Ray Casting](52-ray-casting.md) or [Digital Compositing](53-digital-compositing.md), FDVR produces line-integral projections without hidden surface effects or direct transparency control, making it suitable for interactive X-ray simulation and medical imaging where occlusion is not required.

### [GPU-based 2D FFT](841-gpu-based-2d-fft.md)
[GPU-based 2D FFT](#841-gpu-based-2d-fft.md) is a hardware-accelerated method for computing the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) on graphics processing units, specifically adapted for the domain-transform pipeline of volume rendering. It solves the computational bottleneck of transforming 2D projection slices between the frequency and spatial domains by exploiting the separability of the 2D DFT into two 1D passes. It sets itself apart from CPU-based FFTs by utilizing texture memory and fragment shaders for parallel butterfly operations, and from [direct spatial convolution](#2513-spatial-convolution.md) by operating in the frequency domain to enable efficient projection-slice extraction.

### [Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction](895-hartley-transform-for-memory-reduction.md)
Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction is a frequency-domain volume rendering technique that replaces the standard Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) with the Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) to map real-valued spatial data directly to real-valued spectra. This eliminates the need for complex number arithmetic, thereby reducing memory requirements by half compared to storing a full complex spectrum, and by a factor of 16 compared to double-precision complex Fourier transforms. It sets itself apart from standard Fourier-based frequency rendering by avoiding the complexity of handling Hermitian symmetry during slice extraction, which would otherwise be required to save memory in the Fourier domain. It builds on [Domain-transform methods](28-domain-transform-methods.md) by providing the specific spectral representation and memory optimization strategies.

### [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering](952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md)
[Frequency Domain Volume Rendering](#952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md) (FVR) is a volume rendering technique that transforms scalar data from the spatial domain to the frequency domain, extracts a 2D projection slice, and inverse-transforms the result to the spatial domain, thereby avoiding the $O(N^3)$ computational complexity of spatial projection methods. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on the Projection-Slice Theorem to decouple the rendering step from the dataset resolution, allowing the rendering performance to depend primarily on the output image resolution rather than the input volume size.

### [Domain Repetition](1218-domain-repetition.md)
[Domain Repetition](#1218-domain-repetition.md) is a technique for creating infinite, periodic repetitions of an object in space by wrapping query coordinates using modulo arithmetic. It allows rendering an infinite grid of primitives "for free" by modifying the position before querying the base signed distance field ([SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md)). Unlike [Polar Modulo](3358-polar-modulo.md), which repeats objects in a polar/cylindrical arrangement, [Space Repetition](#1677-space-repetition.md) tiles space with a rectangular (Cartesian) cell structure.

### [Fourier Transform](2288-fourier-transform.md)
The Fourier Transform method converts a 3D scalar volume into the frequency domain to enable rendering via the Projection-Slice Theorem. It differs from spatial-domain methods by performing a global transformation of the entire volume, which allows for efficient convolution operations but requires significant preprocessing memory and does not support interactive parameter changes like opacity or lighting.

### [Translation-invariant Fluorescence Rendering via Fourier Convolution](5085-translation-invariant-fluorescence-rendering-via-fourier-con.md)
This method renders 3D fluorescence microscopy images by convolving a parameterized fluorophore density with a translation-invariant Point Spread Function (PSF) in the Fourier domain. It solves the problem of differentiable 3D image synthesis, enabling the optimization of both the biological sample's geometry and the microscope's optical parameters by minimizing the distance between rendered and ground-truth images. Unlike [standard volume rendering](#1165-standard-volume-rendering-equation.md) which integrates opacity along rays, this approach models the physical blurring of the imaging system, allowing for gradient-based inference of shape and optical properties.

### [DCT-based Volume Rendering](5396-dct-based-volume-rendering.md)
[DCT-based Volume Rendering](#5396-dct-based-volume-rendering.md) is a domain-transform method that represents a 3D scalar volume using cosine waves as basis functions, mapping real input values to real output values. It differs from its siblings, such as [Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering](#824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md) and Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction, primarily in its handling of the compression domain: while DFT and DHT support direct rendering from the frequency domain, [DCT](#8014-discrete-cosine-transform-dct.md) does not. Instead, it requires on-demand decompression of data blocks during the rendering pipeline. It is often chosen in practice because it offers independent bases and fast forward/inverse transforms.

### [Hartley Transform](6324-hartley-transform.md)
The Hartley Transform is a real-valued integral transform that maps a real input function to a real spectrum, serving as an alternative to the complex Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for real-valued data. In volume rendering, it enables domain-transform methods (such as Fourier volume rendering) to operate entirely in the real domain, avoiding complex arithmetic while preserving the projection-slice theorem. It is distinguished from its sibling [Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering](824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md) by using the Hartley kernel ($\cos + \sin$) instead of the complex exponential ($\cos + i\sin$), which simplifies implementation for real-valued signals and reduces memory overhead for intermediate representations.

### [Frequency-Domain Methods](9801-frequency-domain-methods.md)
Frequency-Domain Methods represent volumetric data (including dynamic 4D [spacetime](#7334-spacetime.md) volumes) as a superposition of basis functions in the frequency domain, often utilizing tensor [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) to reduce memory usage. Unlike spatial-domain methods that store values at grid points, this approach stores spectral coefficients. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering](824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md) by focusing on explicit spectral representation and decomposition for compact storage rather than projection-slice extraction for rendering, and from [DCT-based Volume Rendering](5396-dct-based-volume-rendering.md) by using complex exponential Fourier bases instead of discrete cosine bases.

## Background
Domain-transform methods, also known as Fourier-space techniques, were introduced to address the computational limitations of spatial-domain volume rendering [S1, unofficial]. The basic idea is to compute the 3D Fourier transformation of the entire volume in a pre-processing step, extract a slice image in the frequency domain, and transform it back into the spatial domain using the 2D inverse Fourier transformation [S1, unofficial]. The main advantage is the computational complexity of $O(N^2)$ for the projection, disregarding the one-time 3D Fourier transformation pre-processing step [S1, unofficial]. The major drawback is that they do not allow an interactive modification of any display parameter other than the viewing direction [S1, unofficial]. These methods fall under the broader category of domain methods, where spatial data is transformed into an alternative domain (such as compression, wavelet, or frequency domain) from which a projection is directly generated [S2].
